item.title: FOSSLight
item.description:
FOSSLight is an open source project led by LG Electronics. It analyzes source code, binaries, and dependencies using various scanners to generate an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials). FOSSLight Hub provides open source management, license management, and vulnerability management features to support the compliance process.

  • Official website: https://fosslight.org/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/fosslight/fosslight_hub
  • License: Apache-2.0

1. Features

  • Multiple scanner integration: Integrates ScanCode Toolkit, SPDX Tools, CycloneDX, FOSSology, and other open source scanners
  • Wide scan target support: Source code, binaries, container images, Linux packages, and more
  • SBOM generation and management: Creates and manages SBOMs in various formats (SPDX, CycloneDX, Excel, Text)
  • License detection and management: Accurately detects and manages open source license information
  • Vulnerability integration: Links to external vulnerability databases such as NVD and CVE
  • FOSSLight Hub: Web-based UI providing open source management, license management, and vulnerability management

2. Installation

FOSSLight consists of FOSSLight Scanner and FOSSLight Hub. The easiest way to install both is using Docker Compose.

item.title: OSV-SCALIBR
item.description:
OSV-SCALIBR (Open Source Vulnerabilities - Software Composition Analysis LIBRary) is an open source software composition analysis tool developed by Google. It scans filesystems, container images, and binaries to identify included packages and detects known vulnerabilities by cross-referencing the OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) database. It also supports SBOM generation in SPDX format.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/google/osv-scalibr
  • License: Apache-2.0

1. Features

  • Multiple scan targets: Local filesystem, container images, archive files
  • Wide ecosystem support: Go, Python, Java (Maven), JavaScript (npm), Rust, Ruby, and more
  • OSV DB integration: Cross-references scan results with the OSV database to provide CVE and other vulnerability information
  • SBOM output: Exports results in SPDX 2.3 format
  • CLI and library: Provided as both a standalone binary (CLI) and a Go library

2. Installation

Build with Go 1.21 or later:

item.title: cdxgen
item.description:
cdxgen is an open source SBOM generation tool managed by OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project). It analyzes source code, build artifacts, and container images to automatically generate SBOMs in CycloneDX format.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/CycloneDX/cdxgen
  • License: Apache-2.0

Features

  • Wide language and ecosystem support: Java (Maven/Gradle), Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, .NET, and 20+ more
  • Multiple scan targets: Source code directories, container images, GitHub repositories
  • CycloneDX standard output: Supports CycloneDX 1.4/1.5/1.6 in JSON and XML formats
  • REPL mode: Interactive interface for exploring and querying SBOMs
  • CI/CD integration: Easy integration with GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and other major pipelines

Installation

Install with Node.js 18 or later:

item.title: ISO 5230, 18974, and 42001 Comparison
item.description:
1. Relationship Among the Three Standards

A company that develops AI systems using open source stands at the point where three standards intersect.

flowchart LR
 subgraph oss["Open source management"]
 A["ISO/IEC 5230\nLicense compliance\n(licenses, SBOM, artifacts)"]
 B["ISO/IEC 18974\nSecurity assurance\n(vulnerability detection, response, CVD)"]
 end

 subgraph ai["AI system management"]
 C["ISO/IEC 42001\nAI management system\n(governance, risk, life cycle)"]
 end

 oss -- "Open source compliance\nwithin AI systems" --> ai

ISO 5230 and 18974 are standards for managing open source itself, while ISO 42001 is a standard for managing AI systems. The two areas are independent, but they intersect when AI systems use open source.

item.title: Syft
item.description:
Syft is an open source SBOM generation CLI tool developed by Anchore. It scans container images, filesystems, and archives to identify included packages and generates SBOMs in SPDX or CycloneDX format.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/anchore/syft
  • License: Apache-2.0

Features

  • Multiple scan targets: Container images (Docker, OCI), local filesystems, tar archives
  • Wide ecosystem support: Alpine (apk), Debian/Ubuntu (dpkg), RPM, Python, Java, Go, Node.js, Ruby, Rust, and more
  • Standard output formats: SPDX 2.2/2.3 (JSON, tag-value), CycloneDX 1.4/1.5 (JSON, XML), Syft JSON
  • Grype integration: Pairs naturally with Anchore’s Grype vulnerability scanner for SBOM-based vulnerability analysis
  • Easy installation: Single binary distribution, no additional runtime required

Installation

Script Installation (Linux/macOS)

curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin

Homebrew (macOS)

brew install syft

Docker

docker pull anchore/syft

Basic Usage

(1) Scan a Container Image

# Scan a Docker image and output SPDX JSON
syft ubuntu:22.04 -o spdx-json=sbom.spdx.json

# Output as CycloneDX JSON
syft ubuntu:22.04 -o cyclonedx-json=sbom.cdx.json

(2) Scan a Local Directory

syft dir:/path/to/project -o spdx-json=sbom.spdx.json

(3) View Results in Terminal

# Print package list to terminal
syft ubuntu:22.04

# Output as JSON to stdout
syft ubuntu:22.04 -o json

(4) Vulnerability Scanning with Grype

# Generate SBOM with Syft and analyze vulnerabilities with Grype
syft ubuntu:22.04 -o json | grype

CI/CD Integration Example

# GitHub Actions example
- name: Generate SBOM with Syft
 uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
 with:
 image: myapp:latest
 format: spdx-json
 output-file: sbom.spdx.json
- name: Upload SBOM
 uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
 with:
 name: sbom
 path: sbom.spdx.json

References

  • Syft GitHub: https://github.com/anchore/syft
  • Grype (vulnerability scanner): https://github.com/anchore/grype
  • SPDX Standard: https://spdx.dev/
  • CycloneDX Standard: https://cyclonedx.org/

item.title: Dependency-Track
item.description:
Dependency-Track is an open source SBOM management and vulnerability analysis platform managed by OWASP. It continuously monitors component-level vulnerabilities based on uploaded SBOMs (CycloneDX, SPDX) and automatically evaluates policy violations.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/DependencyTrack/dependency-track
  • Official docs: https://docs.dependencytrack.org/
  • License: Apache-2.0

Features

  • SBOM-based continuous monitoring: Automatically tracks the latest vulnerabilities per component after uploading SBOMs in SPDX or CycloneDX format
  • Multiple vulnerability data sources: NVD, OSV, GitHub Advisories, VulnDB, and more
  • Policy engine: Define rules for license policies, vulnerability severity thresholds, and component allowlists for automatic evaluation
  • REST API: Integrate with CI/CD pipelines to automatically upload SBOMs and receive feedback at build time
  • Web UI dashboard: View per-project risk scores, vulnerability status, and license distribution at a glance
  • Notifications: Send new vulnerability alerts via Slack, email, Webhook, and other channels

Installation

Using Docker Compose is the simplest approach:

item.title: Building an Automated Open Source Management Environment: cdxgen + Dependency-Track
item.description:
For companies just starting with open source management, we recommend the cdxgen + Dependency-Track combination as a toolset that can establish a basic automation environment within a single day.

This guide walks you through every step, from installation and configuration to setting up a license and vulnerability inspection environment and running day-to-day operations.

Why cdxgen + Dependency-Track

Open source management comes down to two essentials.

  1. Know what is inside — generating an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)
  2. Continuously monitor risk — detecting vulnerabilities (CVEs) and license policy violations

cdxgen handles the first, and Dependency-Track handles the second. Both tools are free open source under the Apache-2.0 license.

item.title: SCANOSS
item.description:
SCANOSS is a Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tool that can identify open source components not only at the file level but down to the snippet (code fragment) level. It detects license and copyright information by matching against a knowledge base (OSSKB, Open Source Knowledge Base) that indexes more than 100 million files, and automatically generates SBOMs in CycloneDX and SPDX formats.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/scanoss
  • Official site: https://www.scanoss.com
  • License: Apache-2.0

1. Key features

  • Snippet-level matching: Can trace the origin even when a portion of code, rather than an entire file, has been copied or modified
  • Large-scale knowledge base: OSSKB indexes more than 100 million open source files — covering major package repositories and GitHub
  • Automatic SBOM generation: Supports CycloneDX (JSON/XML) and SPDX format output
  • Both CLI & REST API: Provides both the scanoss-py (Python) CLI and a REST API, making automation integration easy
  • CI/CD pipeline integration: Can scan with a single command in CI environments such as GitHub Actions

2. Installation

Install via pip in a Python 3.8 or later environment.

item.title: §3.1.1 Policy
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

A company without an Open Source Policy risks distributing software while developers are unaware of their open source license obligations. This can lead to serious legal and business risks, such as copyright infringement lawsuits, mandatory source code disclosure, and termination of business contracts. §3.1.1 requires organizations to establish a documented policy governing open source license compliance for supplied software and to communicate it so that all Program Participants within the organization are aware of the policy’s existence. This clause forms the foundation of the entire ISO/IEC 5230 program; all subsequent clauses (competence, processes, artifacts, etc.) operate on top of this policy.

item.title: §3.2.1 External Inquiry Response
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

Companies distributing software may receive inquiries from third parties (customers, open source copyright holders, researchers, etc.) regarding open source license compliance. Failure to respond to these inquiries in a timely manner risks escalation into copyright infringement disputes. §3.2.1 requires organizations to establish a publicly available means of contact for receiving external inquiries and to document a procedure internally for systematically responding to those inquiries. This clause requires both a public channel (Verification Material 3.2.1.1) and an internal response procedure (Verification Material 3.2.1.2).

item.title: §3.3.1 SBOM
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

Without knowing what open source components are included in the supplied software, it is impossible to fulfill license obligations or respond to security vulnerabilities. §3.3.1 requires the establishment of a procedure for identifying, tracking, reviewing, approving, and archiving the open source components that make up supplied software, and maintaining component records (SBOM) that demonstrate the procedure has actually been followed. This clause forms the foundation for operating the SBOM, which is the core infrastructure of open source license compliance and Security Assurance.

item.title: §3.4.1 Artifacts
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

To fulfill license obligations, Compliance Artifacts such as notices and source code packages must actually be prepared and provided with the software. §3.4.1 requires the establishment of a procedure for preparing the Compliance Artifacts required by the identified licenses and distributing them with the supplied software, as well as a procedure for retaining copies of the artifacts for a certain period. This clause connects the results of the §3.3 review and approval stage to actual distribution and archiving.

item.title: §3.5.1 Contributions
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

Many companies contribute code, documentation, bug reports, and more to external open source projects. Contribution activities build community trust and expand technical influence, but they also carry the risk of unintentionally disclosing company code or patents. §3.5.1 requires organizations that allow external open source contributions to establish a documented policy and procedure governing contributions, and to ensure that Program Participants are aware of their existence. This clause does not apply to organizations that do not allow contributions, but if they do, all three verification materials must be in place.

item.title: §3.6.1 Conformance
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

To receive official recognition of ISO/IEC 5230 conformance, the program defined in §3.1.4 must be confirmed in a document as satisfying all requirements of this specification. §3.6.1 is the stage for officially affirming that all clauses from §3.1 through §3.5 have been satisfied. This clause is the final confirmation procedure that completes adherence to the specification, requiring the organization’s official confirmation that the program satisfies all requirements of ISO/IEC 5230:2020 version 2.1.

item.title: §4.1.1 Policy
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.1.1 corresponds to ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.1 (License Compliance Policy), but the focus shifts to Security Assurance. A policy that systematically manages known and newly discovered vulnerabilities in open source components of the supplied software must be documented and communicated internally. The key difference from ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.1 is the requirement for a periodic review process for the policy itself and its communication method. It is not enough to establish a policy; a review system must be in place to ensure the policy always remains valid and up to date.

item.title: §4.2.1 Access
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.2.1 has the same structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.2.1 (External Inquiry Response), but the focus shifts from license compliance inquiries to vulnerability inquiries. A publicly visible channel must be established for third parties to make inquiries about known or newly discovered vulnerabilities in the supplied software, and an internal procedure for systematically handling these inquiries must be documented. Since the security vulnerability reporting channel is connected to the Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) procedure, a system for safely receiving and processing vulnerabilities discovered by security researchers or customers is required.

item.title: §4.3.1 SBOM
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.3.1 has the same basic structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.3.1 (SBOM), but the emphasis differs. While 5230 covers the SBOM for license management of open source components, §4.3.1 of 18974 emphasizes continuously recording and retaining the SBOM throughout the entire software lifecycle. In particular, the SBOM must be maintained even after deployment so it can be integrated with the vulnerability monitoring in §4.3.2 Security Assurance. Without an SBOM, post-deployment impact analysis for newly published CVEs (§4.1.5 Method 5) cannot be performed.

item.title: §4.4.1 Completeness
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.4.1 corresponds to ISO/IEC 5230 §3.6.1 (Conformance). A document must be prepared affirming that the program defined in §4.1.4 satisfies all requirements of ISO/IEC 18974. The structure is the same as 5230 §3.6.1, but the difference is that the subject of confirmation covers all 25 Verification Material items of 18974. When preparing for ISO/IEC 5230 and 18974 certification simultaneously, it is efficient to conduct an integrated review of the common items of both standards and then additionally confirm the 9 items exclusive to 18974 (marked with ★).

item.title: Closed Network Operation and the Network Separation Transition
item.description:
Where this page fits

This guide covers the use and management of open source in the financial sector. Its starting point is the closed network. Import, internal mirrors, and offline vulnerability management are prerequisites for every stage, including identification, use approval, and management, so they are explained once here, and each stage page points to this page with an “Applying in a closed network” box.

Documents produced here: an import procedure and import approval records, and a self risk assessment for a network separation exception.

item.title: 0. Exploring OpenChain
item.description:
1. What is the OpenChain Project?

Software today is growing ever larger and more complex. Developing a single piece of software may involve not only internally developed code but also open source, third-party software, vendor SDKs, and a wide variety of software across the software supply chain.

If even one organization in this complex software supply chain fails to comply with open source license obligations or does not provide accurate open source information, the company ultimately distributing the software will inevitably fail to meet its open source license compliance obligations. This can lead to lawsuits and the suspension of product sales.

item.title: 1. Context of the Organization and Leadership
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §4 and §5 are the foundation of the AI management system. They determine which AI systems the organization operates, who the interested parties are, and on what principles top management will manage AI.

From the perspective of open source practitioners, §5.2 (AI policy) is the most important point of intersection. Including principles on open source use in the AI policy makes it possible to operate it in an integrated way with the ISO 5230 policy.

item.title: 3.1 Policy
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

In an organization without an AI SBOM policy, developers deploy AI systems without being aware of the license obligations of models and datasets. In AI, what must be tracked goes beyond code. Model weights, training datasets, and the Model Tree of models derived from other models each have their own licenses, and non-standard licenses that restrict the purpose of use, such as the Llama Community License or the RAIL family, are common. Missing these obligations leads to copyright disputes, violations of use restrictions, and termination of business contracts.

item.title: 3.10 Governance
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 4: Governance. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

Governance is the framework that brings all the preceding clauses together and ensures responsible development, deployment, and management across the AI system lifecycle. If the policy (3.1) sets the principles and license obligations (3.5) and the AI SBOM (3.9) create individual processes, governance manages them so that they work consistently even as regulations change and models are replaced.

item.title: 3.5 License Obligations
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

License obligations are where the AI SBOM guide extends ISO/IEC 5230 the most. Whereas traditional open source compliance reviewed the licenses of code, in AI the review targets grow to four: the AI system’s code, model weights, datasets (including training, testing, and verification datasets), and the license of the AI system itself. Because it is common for one model to be derived from several other models, each upstream model in the Model Tree has its own license.

item.title: 3.7 Access
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 3: Operating Structure. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

Organizations that exchange AI systems in the supply chain need to confirm each other’s compliance. For that, a channel for external inquiries must be publicly available, and the organization must be ready to respond to those inquiries. Access ensures both directions.

3.7 requires two things: publicly identifying a means by which a third party can make an AI SBOM compliance inquiry, and maintaining an internal process to respond effectively to those inquiries. For AI, inquiries also cover AI-specific information such as model and dataset licenses, training data provenance, and model cards.

item.title: ISO/IEC 5230 Conformance Guide
item.description:
This guide walks through each requirement clause of ISO/IEC 5230 (OpenChain License Compliance) one by one. It explains what verification materials each clause requires, how to comply, and what sample documents can be used directly.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

Target Audience

  • Open source compliance officers and open source program managers
  • Personnel at companies preparing for ISO/IEC 5230 certification
  • Practitioners who want to review their existing open source management framework against ISO standards

How to Use This Guide

Relationship with the Enterprise Open Source Management Guide

The Enterprise Open Source Management Guide explains how to implement open source management in practice (policies, processes, tools, and organization).

This guide (ISO/IEC 5230 Conformance Guide) organizes, clause by clause, what must be demonstrated for certification.

Guide Focus When to Use
Enterprise Open Source Management Guide Practical implementation (How to implement) When building an open source management framework from scratch
ISO/IEC 5230 Conformance Guide Verification material criteria by clause (What to prove) When preparing for certification or conducting a self-assessment

The two guides are complementary. Each clause page provides cross-links to the corresponding section of the Enterprise Open Source Management Guide.

item.title: onot
item.description:
An open source notice file is a compliance artifact that provides users with copyright and license information for open source components included in supplied software. Writing notice files manually is error-prone and time-consuming. onot automates this process.

SK Telecom developed onot internally and released it as open source under the name onot. Kakao also contributed major features through collaborative development.

Features

onot takes an SBOM in SPDX format as input and automatically converts it into an open source notice file. It is Python-based, lightweight, and easy to use.

item.title: Open Source Management in AI Systems
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8.5 (AI system life cycle) and §8.6 (AI data management) cover requirements that must be managed during the AI system development stage. From an open source perspective, the key is license compliance for the open source components used in AI systems.

2. §8.5 AI System Life Cycle: Managing Open Source Frameworks and Models

2.1 Planning and Design Stage

When selecting the open source frameworks and models to use in the planning stage of an AI system, review their licenses in advance.

item.title: OWASP AIBOM Generator
item.description:
Overview

OWASP AIBOM Generator is an open source tool that takes a Hugging Face model ID, retrieves the model card metadata, and generates an AI SBOM in CycloneDX format. It is maintained by the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, and its distinguishing feature is scoring how complete the generated BOM is.

Unlike cdxgen, which identifies dependencies quickly but leaves licenses empty, this tool fills in the license, authors, and external references written in the model card. It is a good starting point for the license review required by 3.5 License Obligations.

item.title: Program Foundation
item.description: This is Phase 1 of the implementation roadmap. It defines the scope of the program (3.4), establishes the policy (3.1), and secures the competence and awareness of participants (3.2, 3.3). All subsequent clauses operate on this foundation.

item.title: Self-Check Workbook
item.description:
This workbook turns the check items on the Self-Check page into a form for recording. Its purpose is to go beyond checking: for the areas that fall short, record the owner and deadline so that the results lead into an improvement plan.

How to use

Mark the compliance status of each item at one of three levels.

  • Not met: There is no related activity or document.
  • Partially met: The activity exists, but documents or records are insufficient.
  • Met: Both the activity and the supporting documents are in place.

For partially met or unmet items, write what the supporting document should be, and who will put it in place by when. For met items, write the name and location of the supporting document so that it can be used directly as verification material for ISO self-certification.

item.title: TRUSCA
item.description:
Managing the vulnerabilities and licenses of open source components calls for an SCA (Software Composition Analysis) tool. Several commercial products exist, but some organizations look for an open source tool they can install and run on their own infrastructure.

TRUSCA is a self-hosted SCA portal published for that purpose. Released under Apache 2.0, it brings vulnerabilities (CVE), license compliance, and SBOM management into a single screen. It is developed by Trusted OSS, a project that grew out of KWG community work.

item.title: §3.1.2 Competence
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

For an open source program to actually function, the people assigned to relevant roles must have the competence to perform those roles. If roles and responsibilities are only written in documents and the people responsible have no basic knowledge of open source license or security vulnerability management, the policies and processes will be nominal. §3.1.2 requires the organization to identify the roles involved in the program, define the competence required for each role, evaluate and record whether participants actually possess that competence. This clause advances the role structure defined in §3.1.1 Policy into a concrete competence framework.

item.title: §3.2.2 Effective Resources
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

For an open source program to actually function, it is not enough to just define roles. Actual personnel must be assigned to each role, and sufficient time and budget must be provided to carry out the work. §3.2.2 requires organizations to document the persons responsible for each program role, confirm that staffing and budget are appropriately allocated, and to have a method for accessing legal expertise, a procedure for assigning internal responsibilities, and a procedure for handling non-compliance cases. This clause consists of five verification material items and is the stage that implements the role structure defined in §3.1 Program Foundation into an actual operational framework.

item.title: §3.3.2 License Compliance
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

License obligations for open source components vary depending on the distribution format (binary, source code), whether modifications were made, and how they are combined with other components. §3.3.2 requires the program to have the capability to handle the common open source license use cases for open source components in the supplied software. This clause goes beyond simply identifying licenses to establishing procedures that define how to fulfill obligations for various distribution scenarios.

item.title: §3.6.2 Duration
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

ISO/IEC 5230 conformance does not remain valid indefinitely once obtained. When a new version of the specification is published, a program that was conformant against the previous version retains its conformance for only 18 months after the new version is published. §3.6.2 requires organizations to maintain a document confirming that the program meets all requirements of the specification within the past 18 months of obtaining conformance. This clause serves as a mechanism to ensure that open source compliance programs remain continuously operational rather than stopping at formal certification.

item.title: §4.1.2 Competence
item.description:
★ 18974 Exclusive Items — Documented Evidence Strength

§4.1.2.3·§4.1.2.5·§4.1.2.6 are ISO 18974 exclusive (★) items requiring Documented Evidence. A simple procedure document is insufficient — you must retain actual execution records (participant list, review meeting minutes, internal best practice comparison results). For a detailed explanation of the strength difference, see §4.1.5 Standard Practices — Documented Evidence Notice.

1. Clause Overview

§4.1.2 has the same basic structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.2 (Competence), but requires 3 additional Verification Material items. While 5230 requires three items — a list of roles, a definition of competencies per role, and evidence of competency assessment — 18974 additionally requires a list of participants and their role mappings (4.1.2.3), evidence of periodic review and process changes (4.1.2.5), and verification of alignment with internal best practices (4.1.2.6). These three additional items require demonstrating that the competence framework is not merely formal, but is actively kept up to date and aligned with industry standards.

item.title: §4.2.2 Effectively Resourced
item.description:
★ 18974 Exclusive Items — Documented Evidence Strength

§4.2.2.3 is an ISO 18974 exclusive (★) item requiring Documented Evidence. The method for accessing vulnerability resolution resources is not merely a procedure document — you must retain actual resource utilization records (security advisory contracts, account issuance records, access logs). For a detailed explanation of the strength difference, see §4.1.5 Standard Practices — Documented Evidence Notice.

1. Clause Overview

§4.2.2 corresponds to ISO/IEC 5230 §3.2.2 (Effectively Resourced) but has two key differences. First, while 5230 requires 5 Verification Materials, 18974 requires 4. The §3.2.2.5 item from 5230 (procedure for reviewing and correcting non-compliance cases) is absorbed into §4.1.5 Standard Practice Implementation in 18974. Second, §3.2.2.3 (method for accessing legal expertise) is replaced in §4.2.2.3 by vulnerability resolution expertise. Rather than legal expertise for license matters, the organization must secure technical and security expertise capable of actually resolving known vulnerabilities and document how that expertise is accessed.

item.title: §4.3.2 Security Assurance
item.description:
★ 18974 Exclusive Items — Documented Evidence Strength

§4.3.2.1·§4.3.2.2 are ISO 18974 exclusive (★) items requiring Documented Evidence. Not merely a “vulnerability response procedure document,” but actual execution records for each CVE (scan results, CVSS scores, remediation history, VEX issuance, customer notification history) must be retained. For a detailed explanation of the strength difference, see §4.1.5 Standard Practices — Documented Evidence Notice.

1. Clause Overview

§4.3.2 is the core clause of ISO/IEC 18974 and is a new clause exclusive to 18974 that does not exist in ISO/IEC 5230. It requires establishing a procedure covering the entire process — vulnerability detection → risk assessment → remediation decision → customer consent (where applicable) → remediation → post-deployment newly disclosed vulnerability response → continuous monitoring — for each open source component in the SBOM, and maintaining implementation records. If §4.1.5 requires the existence of vulnerability handling methods, §4.3.2 requires that those methods have actually been applied to each component with records retained.

item.title: §4.4.2 Duration
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.4.2 has the same structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.6.2 (Duration). It requires organizations to maintain a retrospective document confirming that all requirements of the specification have been met during the past 18 months of obtaining conformance (this is a past-fact confirmation, not a future commitment). When a new version of the specification is published, conformance under the previous version is maintained for a grace period of 18 months, during which it is recommended to update to the latest version.

item.title: Governance: Management Organization and Approval System
item.description:
Where this page fits

Governance is the foundation of open source management. The identification, use approval, and management stages work only after you decide who is responsible, who reviews, and who approves. The FSEC guide also covers the composition and roles of the management organization separately, before the management procedures.

Documents produced here: an open source policy, a list of roles and responsibilities, and records of role assignments.

Where does financial sector governance start?

The “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022, hereafter the FSEC guide) presents the composition and operation of the management organization and examples of roles. ISO/IEC 5230 requires these as verification materials: a documented policy (3.1.1.1), a list of roles and responsibilities (3.1.2.1), identification of the people in each role (3.2.2.1), and a method for accessing legal expertise (3.2.2.3). Governance is the activity that produces these verification materials.

item.title: 2. Planning
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §6 requires a systematic way to identify and address risks and opportunities related to AI systems. In particular, §6.1.2 (AI risk assessment) and §6.1.4 (AI system impact assessment) are used directly to include risks that can arise from open source components.

2. §6.1.2 AI Risk Assessment: Including Open Source Risks ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires a process to identify, analyze, and evaluate risks related to AI systems. Open source practitioners must explicitly include open source license risks and security vulnerability risks in this process.

item.title: 3.2 Competence
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If the policy (3.1) sets out what must be done, competence ensures there are people who can do it. AI SBOM compliance requires broader knowledge than open source compliance, which dealt only with code licenses. Practitioners must judge the licenses of model weights and datasets, interpret model cards, and understand emerging AI regulations and the use restrictions of non-standard licenses.

item.title: 3.6 Transparency Obligations
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If license obligations (3.5) ask “do we have the right to use this material,” transparency obligations ask “what must we disclose about this material.” The two obligations come from different sources. License obligations are imposed by copyright holders through contract, and transparency obligations are imposed by regulations through law.

3.6 requires a procedure for reviewing whether there are transparency obligations imposed by regulations. The review covers training, testing, and verification datasets and takes into account the intended use of the model. If the use case for the training data creates a transparency issue (e.g., disclosure obligations to downstream recipients), appropriate risk mitigation measures must be taken. As the EU AI Act begins to fully apply its transparency obligations from August 2026, this clause is becoming more important in practice.

item.title: 3.8 Effectively Resourced
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 3: Operating Structure. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If competence (3.2) defines “who must be able to do what,” effective resourcing attaches actual people, time, and budget to those roles so that the program works. If policies and procedures exist only on paper with no resources, compliance exists in name only.

3.8 requires assigning accountability for program tasks and allocating sufficient resources. There are five verification materials, covering identification of role owners, provision of staff and funding, access to legal expertise, a procedure for assigning internal responsibilities, and a procedure for remediating non-compliance. The specification cites the resource-related sections (B.4.2, B.4.6) and the human oversight section (B.9.3) of Annex B of ISO/IEC 42001 as references.

item.title: AI Extension Processes
item.description: This is Phase 2 of the implementation roadmap. It is the area where the AI SBOM guide extends ISO/IEC 5230 the most, and it covers license obligations (3.5), transparency obligations (3.6), and AI SBOM creation and management (3.9).

item.title: AI SBOM
item.description:
1. What is an AI SBOM?

An AI SBOM (AI System Bill of Materials) documents a list of every element that makes up an AI system, along with its source and license. It extends the concept of the software SBOM (ISO/IEC 5230 §3.3.1) to AI systems and is the key deliverable for the ISO/IEC 42001 §7.5 (Documented information) requirement.

Why an AI SBOM Is Needed: Transparency and Regulatory Compliance

The AI SBOM is a key means of securing transparency and explainability of AI systems. ISO/IEC 42001 Appendix C.2.11 states transparency and explainability as key objectives of the AI management system.

item.title: cdxgen
item.description:
Overview

cdxgen is the official SBOM generator of the OWASP CycloneDX project. It supports more than 20 languages and package managers, and recent versions provide a dedicated AI BOM mode. It automatically identifies the dependencies of AI applications (PyTorch, Transformers, etc.) and integrates well with CI/CD pipelines.

From an AI SBOM perspective, cdxgen’s strengths are speed and automation. Its weakness is that it does not fill in license information in a default run. The run results below show this characteristic. Whereas OWASP AIBOM Generator centers on model card metadata, cdxgen centers on code and dependencies. Using both together covers both models and dependencies.

item.title: ISO/IEC 18974 Conformance Guide
item.description:
This guide explains each requirement clause of ISO/IEC 18974 (OpenChain Security Assurance) one by one. It describes what Verification Materials each clause requires, how to comply, and what sample documents can be used immediately.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

Target Audience

  • Security managers and open source program managers at organizations establishing an open source security assurance framework for the first time
  • Engineers building open source vulnerability management processes in DevSecOps environments
  • Organization staff preparing to add ISO/IEC 18974 certification after obtaining ISO/IEC 5230 certification

Relationship with ISO/IEC 5230

ISO/IEC 18974 adds a security layer on top of ISO/IEC 5230

ISO/IEC 5230 (License Compliance) covers the foundational program for systematically managing open source license obligations.

ISO/IEC 18974 (Security Assurance) adds a security layer of vulnerability detection, assessment, and response on top of that foundation. The two standards share core infrastructure such as policy, competence, and SBOM, and 18974 extends and deepens this from a security perspective.

Category ISO/IEC 5230 ISO/IEC 18974
Purpose License Compliance Security Assurance
Verification Materials 24 items 25 items
Common Foundation Clauses — 16 (corresponding to 5230)
18974-Exclusive Clauses — 9 (security-specific)
Key Additional Elements — Vulnerability detection, response, and CVD procedures

item.title: Policy and Procedure Templates
item.description:
The forms here are outlines that add items specific to the financial sector. For general open source policy and process forms, use the existing policy and procedure templates guide, and use the forms below for what the financial sector additionally needs: import control, risk assessment for network separation exceptions, and SBOM requirements for outsourcing.

How to use

The outlines below are not finished documents to use as they are, but frames to fill in. Replace the parts in square brackets to suit your organization. Have them reviewed by your internal legal and security teams before issuing them.

item.title: §3.1.3 Awareness
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

Even participants with the right roles and competencies will only participate in a perfunctory manner if they do not understand the purpose of the open source program and the meaning of their own contribution to the overall compliance framework. §3.1.3 requires the organization to evaluate and record that Program Participants actually understand the program’s objectives, how they contribute, and the consequences of failing to follow the program’s requirements. This clause is the next step after §3.1.2 Competence (possessing knowledge and skills), forming the practical motivation by connecting the competence participants hold to the program’s purpose.

item.title: §4.1.3 Awareness
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

§4.1.3 has the same Verification Material structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.3 (Awareness). It requires that awareness of program objectives, how individuals contribute to the program, and the implications of non-compliance be assessed and recorded for Program Participants. The difference from 5230 is that the focus of the awareness assessment shifts to Security Assurance. Participants must be aware not only of license compliance but also of the vulnerability management process, CVD procedures, and CVSS-based response criteria.

item.title: Identification: Finding All the Open Source You Use
item.description:
Where this page fits

Identification is the starting point of management. If you do not know what you use, you cannot manage its vulnerabilities or license obligations. It is the first procedure in the “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022, hereafter the FSEC guide) and the activity that SBOM management in ISO/IEC 5230 (3.3.1) requires.

Documents produced here: SBOMs and an inventory of production assets.

item.title: 3. Support
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §7 covers the competence, awareness, communication, and documentation needed to operate the AI management system. From the perspective of open source practitioners, §7.2 (Competence) and §7.5 (Documented information) are the key points of intersection.

2. §7.2 Competence: AI Open Source Management Competence ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires that persons performing AI-related roles have the necessary competence. From an open source compliance perspective, AI development and operations staff should have the following competencies.

item.title: 3.3 Awareness
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If competence (3.2) deals with “can they do it,” awareness deals with “do they know why they must do it.” It is not enough for participants to know only that the policy exists. Compliance actually works only when they also know how their work contributes to the program and what happens if they do not follow it.

item.title: 3.9 AI SBOM
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 2: AI Extension Processes. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

An AI SBOM (AI System Bill of Materials) is a list of the components that make up an AI system and information about them. Whereas a traditional SBOM records software components, an AI SBOM adds models, weights, datasets, and hyperparameters. 3.9 requires a procedure for creating and managing an AI SBOM.

item.title: AI Supply Chain Verification
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8.8 requires appropriate evaluation and verification when using AI systems (models, APIs, services) procured externally. From an open source perspective, the key is the procedure for verifying license, security, and supply chain risks when procuring external open source AI models.

2. Three Types of External AI Procurement

Type Examples Open source relevance
Direct use of open source AI models Downloading Llama, Mistral, or Falcon model weights High: the license applies directly
AI services based on open source Hugging Face Inference API, Ollama Medium: the license of the underlying model must be checked
Commercial AI APIs OpenAI API, Google Vertex AI Low: terms of service apply (OSS licenses do not apply directly)

Types 1 and 2 are areas where open source licenses apply directly and are the main subjects of §3 to §4. Type 3 (commercial AI APIs) is also required in the same way by ISO/IEC 42001 §8.8, so it is covered separately in §5.

item.title: Audit Evidence List
item.description:
The financial sector must keep evidence of its open source management activities to prepare for internal and external audits and for information technology (IT) inspections by the Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원). Because check records from the management step serve directly as evidence, do not create it separately; collect the records that come out of everyday activities in a systematic way. For more context, see Management.

Evidence checklist

The evidence below overlaps with the verification materials of ISO/IEC 5230 and 18974. Documents created while preparing for ISO self-certification serve directly as audit evidence. Set the storage location and retention period according to your organization’s rules.

item.title: ISO/IEC 42001 Guide
item.description:
This guide explains, from the perspective of open source practitioners, the key requirements of ISO/IEC 42001 (AI Management System) that intersect with open source management. It provides practical guidance on what must be complied with when using open source frameworks, pre-trained models, and training datasets in AI systems, and on how to structure an AI SBOM.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is an international standard for an AI management system (AIMS, AI Management System) that enables organizations to develop, operate, and manage AI systems responsibly and transparently.

item.title: Model and Container Scanners (Lab700x, Trivy, Syft)
item.description:
This page introduces analysis and identification tools that complement AI SBOM generation. If the generation tools (OWASP AIBOM Generator, cdxgen) record “what is inside,” these tools look at “whether it is safe” and “which version it is.” The commands and features below are based on each tool’s official documentation (the tools actually run in this guide are OWASP AIBOM Generator and cdxgen).

Lab700x AI SBOM Scanner: Static Analysis of Model Binaries

This tool statically analyzes AI model files themselves to extract information. It examines model binaries such as .safetensors, .pt (PyTorch), and .pkl (Pickle) directly without running them (deep introspection).

item.title: Operations
item.description: This is Phase 3 of the implementation roadmap. You set up a channel for responding to external AI SBOM compliance inquiries (3.7) and assign responsibility, staff, and funding to the program (3.8).

item.title: §3.1.4 Program Scope
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

If it is unclear whether the open source program applies to the entire organization or only to specific product lines or business units, the boundaries of compliance activities become vague and accountability becomes unclear. §3.1.4 requires a documented written statement that clearly defines which software, organizational units, and distribution channels the open source program applies to, and what is outside the scope. The scope may vary depending on the organization’s size and business model, and this clause requires that choice to be explicitly recorded.

item.title: §4.1.4 Program Scope
item.description:
★ 18974 Exclusive Items — Documented Evidence Strength

§4.1.4.2·§4.1.4.3 are ISO 18974 exclusive (★) items requiring Documented Evidence. Metrics must include actual measurement data; continuous improvement must retain review/audit meeting minutes. For a detailed explanation of the strength difference, see §4.1.5 Standard Practices — Documented Evidence Notice.

1. Clause Overview

§4.1.4 is the clause from ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.4 (Program Scope) with 2 additional Verification Materials. While 5230 only requires a written statement that clearly defines the program’s scope, 18974 additionally requires a set of performance metrics the program seeks to improve upon (4.1.4.2) and documented evidence from each review, update, or audit demonstrating continuous improvement (4.1.4.3). These two items are intended to demonstrate that the security assurance program is not static compliance, but a system with measurable goals that continuously improves.

item.title: Identifying and Resolving Issues: Vulnerabilities and Licenses
item.description:
Where this page fits

Once identification has shown what you use, the next step is to resolve the issues that come out of it. There are two kinds of issues: security vulnerabilities and license obligations. This is the second procedure of the FSEC guide, and it corresponds to vulnerability detection and resolution (4.3.2) in ISO/IEC 18974 and to handling license use cases (3.3.2) in ISO/IEC 5230.

Documents produced here: vulnerability remediation records (including VEX), and response deadline criteria by severity.

item.title: 3.4 Program Scope
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

The program scope determines how far compliance applies. If the scope is vague, it becomes unclear for which AI systems an SBOM must be created and which models’ licenses must be reviewed. Only when the scope is declared first do all subsequent clauses know what they apply to.

3.4 requires declaring the scope that applies to each program. Scope can differ from one organization to another. Some organizations cover a single product line, while others cover an entire department or the entire organization. In AI, the scope decision covers not only internally developed models but also models and datasets brought in from outside and the external release of internal models.

item.title: 4. Operation
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8 covers the actual operation stage of the AI management system. From an open source perspective, §8 is the section with the most points of intersection.

Subclause Description Open source intersection
§8.1 Operational planning and control Operating the open source review process
§8.2 to 8.3 AI risk assessment and treatment (during operation) Responding to OSS vulnerability risks
§8.4 AI system impact assessment (during operation) System impact of OSS vulnerabilities
§8.5 AI system life cycle ★ OSS framework and model licenses
§8.6 Data for AI systems ★ Open dataset licenses
§8.7 Feedback interface -
§8.8 Procurement of external AI systems ★ Supply chain verification of external OSS models

2. Detailed Pages

The open source intersection items of this section are covered in detail on the following pages:

item.title: 4. Tools
item.description:
Requirements covered by this section

ISO/IEC 5230: 3.3.1.2
ISO/IEC 18974: 4.3.1.2

1. Source Code Scanning Tools

In the open source identification and inspection stages of the open source process, you can use source code scanning tools. Source code scanning tools help identify the open source included in the supplied software and extract license and copyright information. These tools range from open source-based tools that can be used for free to commercial tools. Each tool has its strengths, but no tool provides a perfect solution to all problems. Therefore, companies should select the appropriate tool that fits the characteristics and requirements of their supplied software.

item.title: Governance
item.description: This is Phase 4 of the implementation roadmap. You bring the preceding clauses together into a governance framework across the AI system lifecycle, and review it periodically to reflect emerging AI regulations (3.10).

item.title: Tool Setup Recipe
item.description:
This recipe is an example of setting up SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation and continuous vulnerability monitoring in a closed network. As a quick starting point, it reorganizes the existing cdxgen and Dependency-Track pipeline tutorial for the financial sector. The purpose is not to recommend a specific product but to show how to build the setup with open source, on-premises tools.

Closed network assumptions

The example below includes a step that downloads tool images. In a closed network, obtain the images and vulnerability databases from outside, move them to the internal container registry and mirror, and configure the tools to pull only from inside. For the import procedure, see Closed Network Operation.

item.title: AI SBOM Compliance Guide
item.description:
This guide explains, one by one, each requirement of AI System Bill of Materials: Compliance Management Guide for the Supply Chain (Version 1.0), published by the OpenChain AI Work Group. It describes what verification materials each clause requires, how to comply, and what samples and tools can be used directly.

This specification carries the structure of the open source license compliance standard ISO/IEC 5230 (requirements, verification materials, rationale) over to the AI supply chain. It brings into the scope of compliance not only code but also the license and transparency obligations of model weights, training datasets, and the Model Tree.

item.title: Practical Guide to Open Source Management in the Financial Sector
item.description:
Financial institutions use more and more open source, yet they must manage it under conditions specific to their sector: closed networks, network separation regulations, supply chain security, and audit response. This guide connects the management procedures set out in the “Guide to Using and Managing Open Source Software in the Financial Sector” (금융분야 오픈소스 소프트웨어 활용·관리 안내서; Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원) and Financial Security Institute (금융보안원), 2022) with the verification materials of the international standards ISO/IEC 5230 and 18974 and with the existing KWG practical guides. It shows practitioners, in an actionable form, what they need to put in place and in what order.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

item.title: §3.1.5 License Obligations
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

The most critical task when including open source components in software is accurately understanding the obligations, restrictions, and rights imposed by the licenses applied to those components. Distributing without reviewing license obligations can result in serious legal risks such as mandatory source code disclosure, missing copyright notices, and patent clause violations. §3.1.5 requires the establishment of a procedure for reviewing all identified licenses to determine their obligations, restrictions, and rights, and for recording the results. This procedure forms the foundation of the §3.3.2 License Compliance process.

item.title: §4.1.5 Standard Practice Implementation
item.description:
Evidence Strength for ISO 18974 Exclusive (★) Items — Documented Evidence

Unlike ISO/IEC 5230, ISO/IEC 18974 requires “Documented Evidence” for its 9 exclusive items (★: §4.1.2.3·4.1.2.5·4.1.2.6·4.1.4.2·4.1.4.3·§4.1.5.1·4.2.2.3·4.3.2.1·4.3.2.2). This is a stronger evidence level than the documented procedure or document required for general items.

Strength ISO Expression Compliance Level Certification Audit
Weak document Artifact existence Format review
Medium documented procedure Documented procedure + intent to follow Procedure body review
Strong Documented Evidence Procedure + records of actual execution (evidence pack) Verification of actual execution evidence: logs, tickets, issue tracking results, etc.

§4.1.5.1 requires not merely “procedure documents” for each of the 8 methods, but also records of activities actually performed (scan logs, tickets, approval history, VEX issuance records, etc.) to pass certification.

item.title: Usage Approval: What to Allow and on What Basis
item.description:
Where this page fits

This is the step where you decide whether to actually use open source that has gone through identification and issue resolution. Approval should not rest on one person’s judgment; it should follow a defined procedure and leave records. This is the third procedure of the FSEC guide, and it connects to license obligation review (3.1.5) and governance in ISO/IEC 5230.

Documents produced here: approval request, review, and decision records, and open source requirement clauses for outsourcing contracts.

item.title: 5. Performance Evaluation and Improvement
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §9 and §10 cover the cycle of confirming whether the AI management system is achieving its intended results and improving where it falls short. From an open source perspective, §9.1 (Monitoring and measurement) is linked with open source compliance metrics.

2. §9.1 Monitoring and Measurement: Open Source Compliance Metrics ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires monitoring and measuring the performance of the AI management system. Integrate existing open source compliance metrics into the performance indicators of the AI management system.

item.title: ISO/IEC 5230 vs 18974 Comparison
item.description:
1. Relationship Between the Two Standards

ISO/IEC 5230 and ISO/IEC 18974 are both international open source standards led by the OpenChain Project, but they address different problems. 5230 covers open source license compliance (fulfillment of copyright obligations, SBOM management, and distribution of Compliance Artifacts), while 18974 covers open source security assurance (vulnerability detection, assessment, response, and CVD). The two standards do not have a complete superset/subset relationship. They share 9 common clauses covering policy, competence, SBOM, and similar areas, but each has its own exclusive clauses — 5230 has clauses for license compliance, artifacts, and contributions, while 18974 has clauses for Standard Practice Implementation and Security Assurance.

item.title: Tools
item.description:
This section covers open source tools that automate AI SBOM compliance. For each tool, it summarizes the main features, installation, and usage, along with actual run results. It makes the categories in the automation maturity map of 3.9 AI SBOM concrete, tool by tool.

There is a limit worth stating plainly. Tools generate BOMs automatically, but they cannot guarantee that the licenses in the generated BOM are correct or that no components are missing. In the tool comparison below, OWASP AIBOM Generator fills in the license from the model card, while cdxgen identifies dependencies quickly but leaves the license field empty. Consider this difference when choosing a tool.

item.title: Trusted OSS
item.description:
Trusted OSS grew out of KWG community work and was published by the author of this guide. Its documentation is released under CC BY 4.0 and its code under MIT and Apache 2.0.

Site: https://trustedoss.github.io/en/

Trusted OSS covers four areas.

Generating self-certification deliverables

It produces the documents required for ISO/IEC 5230 and ISO/IEC 18974 self-certification through a conversation with an AI agent: organizational setup, policy, processes, SBOM analysis, vulnerability reports, training curricula, and a draft conformance statement. It follows the same six steps described in the open source management guide.

item.title: Management: Continuous Checks and Audit Readiness for Internal Operational Systems
item.description:
Where this page fits

Checking once at adoption and stopping there is not management. Open source risk continues throughout operation, and new vulnerabilities are disclosed after adoption. This is the management (monitoring) step, the last procedure of the FSEC guide, and it corresponds to continuous monitoring in ISO/IEC 18974. It is the step with the greatest weight in the financial sector.

Documents produced here: periodic reassessment records, and audit evidence packages.

item.title: Self-Check: Finding the Gaps in Your Program
item.description:
Where this page fits

This page gathers the preceding six steps into a checklist. Go through the items one by one to find the gaps in your program, and move to the section that covers what is missing. The categories are based on the self-check checklist (Appendix 1) of the FSEC guide.

Documents produced here: the self-check workbook (check results and improvement plan).

How to use the self-check

This checklist is not a pass-or-fail test. It is a tool for gauging how far your organization has come and finding what to do next. Just as the FSEC guide is a non-regulatory voluntary check, this checklist is a best-practice baseline. [FSEC guide]

item.title: 7. AI Compliance
item.description:
Requirements Covered in This Section

ISO/IEC 42001: §5.2 (AI Policy) · §6.1.2 (AI Risk Assessment) · §7.5 (Documentation) · §8.5 (AI Lifecycle) · §8.6 (AI Data) · §8.8 (External AI Procurement)

AI systems make extensive use of open source frameworks, pre-trained models, and open datasets. Companies that operate an open source management system (ISO/IEC 5230 · 18974) must apply open source compliance principles during the AI system development phase as well. In addition, development environments that leverage AI coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) require a new management framework to address license contamination and the introduction of vulnerable packages.

item.title: Artifacts: Ready-to-Use Forms and Recipes
item.description:
This guide provides four ready-to-use artifacts along with the main text. Where the main text explains “what to do and why,” the artifacts fill in “in what form to record it.” Each artifact is meant to be adapted to your organization’s situation.

Artifact Use
Self-Check Workbook Combines check items, ISO verification materials, and compliance status, owner, and deadline in a single sheet to find the gaps in your program
Policy and Procedure Templates Provides outlines for a finance-specific policy, an import procedure, a usage approval form, and a self risk assessment report for network separation exceptions
Audit Evidence List Organizes, as a checklist, the evidence required in internal and external audits and supervisory inspections and where it is kept
Tool Setup Recipe Provides an example of setting up and integrating on-premises SBOM and vulnerability tools in a closed network with docker-compose
How to use

The artifacts supplement the existing policy and procedure templates guide for the financial context. Use the existing templates for general practice forms, and use these artifacts together with them for items specific to the financial sector (import control, risk assessment for network separation exceptions, and SBOM requirements for outsourcing).

item.title: Training Slides
item.description:
Training Slides

This page provides a training deck covering the full enterprise open source governance process. It reorganizes the Enterprise Open Source Management Guide into a 4-hour training format.

Open in full screen →

Course Structure

Part Title Key Topics

Part 1 Understanding the Standards ISO/IEC 5230 · 18974 · 42001 + OpenChain
